title: Insert Operators to Hit a Target
statement:
You get a string digits and an integer target. Between any two neighbouring digits you may put +, -, *, or nothing (which glues the digits into one longer number). The digits keep their order.

Return every expression built this way that evaluates to target with the usual precedence: * binds tighter than + and -. A number with more than one digit may not start with 0, so "05" is not allowed, but "0" on its own is.

Write expressions with no spaces. Return them in any order.

examples.why: Both are 6 + 2. Read left to right without precedence, "2+3*2" would be 10, so precedence matters.
"1*05" would also be 5, but 05 has a leading zero, so it is not allowed.
Putting no operator at all is a valid choice.

hints: There are only 4 choices in each of at most 9 gaps. Build the expression left to right and try them all.
The hard part is evaluating as you go. + and − are easy to fold into a running total, but * must apply only to the last term, not to the whole total.
Carry two numbers: the running total and the value of the last term. For *, undo the last term and add last × next: total − last + last × next, and the new last term is last × next.

explain.intuition:
The search itself is plain backtracking: at each position, choose how many digits the next number takes, then choose the operator in front of it. What makes the problem hard is evaluating with precedence while building, without re-parsing every finished string.

The trick is to remember the last term separately from the total. With + and -, the next number becomes a new term. With *, the next number joins the last term: take the last term back out of the total, multiply it, and put it back. For "2+3*2": total 2, then total 5 with last 3, then 5 − 3 + 3·2 = 8 with last 6.
steps: Recurse with (i, expr, total, last): the next unread digit, the text so far, its value, and its last term.
For every end j ≥ i, take part = digits[i..j]. Stop extending if part has more than one digit and starts with 0.
At i = 0, start the expression with part. Otherwise branch three ways: + gives (total + v, v), - gives (total − v, −v), * gives (total − last + last·v, last·v).
When i reaches the end of the digits, keep expr if total == target.
pitfalls: Applying * to the whole running total. That evaluates left to right and accepts wrong expressions like 2+3*2 = 10.
Allowing numbers with a leading zero, such as 05. A lone 0 is fine; 0 followed by more digits is not.
Storing the last term of a subtraction as positive. It must be −v, or a later * undoes the wrong amount.

solutions.title: Generate every string, then evaluate it
solutions.idea: Try all 4ⁿ⁻¹ operator choices, drop strings with leading-zero numbers, and evaluate each one with a small precedence-aware parser.

solutions.title: Backtracking with total and last term
solutions.idea: Build the expression left to right, keeping the running total and the last term so that * can be applied to the last term only.

followups: Add division that must divide exactly. What extra state would you need?
Only count the expressions instead of listing them. Can memoisation help, and on which state?
